html:
Changes to the Roman army traditionally credited to Gaius Marius, above all his decision in 107 BCE to recruit men who owned no property.

Until then a Roman soldier had to own some land, and he served for a campaign and went home to his farm. Needing troops for the Jugurthine War, Marius took volunteers from the poorest citizens, armed at public cost. Other changes are often credited to him too: the cohort of about 480 men as the main unit, the same kit for every legionary, soldiers carrying their own packs (they were nicknamed "Marius's mules"), and the eagle as each legion's standard.

Many historians now doubt that Marius made all these changes, or made them at once. The property rule had been falling for decades, and some changes came later.

The effect is clearer. Soldiers now served for long years and wanted land when they left. The Senate would not give it, as the fate of the Gracchan land law showed, so they looked to their generals. Armies loyal to a man, not to the state, carried Sulla and later Caesar to power. See Roman legion.
sum: Changes to the Roman army traditionally credited to Gaius Marius, above all his decision in 107 BCE to recruit men who owned no property.
